title: Sheinbaum Analyzes Initiative to Prohibit Dual Nationality in the Presidency and Governorships
author: Anahí Del Ángel
content:
_This article by[Anahí Del Ángel](https://contralinea.com.mx/author/anahida/)
originally appeared in the [August 25, 2026 edition of
Contralínea](https://contralinea.com.mx/interno/semana/sheinbaum-analiza-
iniciativa-para-prohibir-doble-nacionalidad-en-presidencia-y-gubernaturas/), a
Mexican investigative journalism magazine._

The federal government is analyzing the possibility of sending the **Congress
of the Union** a **constitutional reform** initiative to restrict candidacies
for the **presidency of the Republic** and for governorships to people with
**dual nationality** , President **Claudia Sheinbaum Pardo** announced.

During her press conference, the President proposed that those who hold these
positions must exclusively represent Mexico’s interests, and so she deemed it
necessary to review the current provisions on the nationality of candidates
for elected office. “We should prohibit it; **a Mexican president is Mexican,
they do not represent another country**.”

> A Mexican president is Mexican; they do not represent another country.
>
> Claudia Sheinbaum

The proposal arose when she was asked about the case of the former governor of
Tamaulipas, **Francisco Javier Cabeza de Vaca** , who holds dual **Mexican and
U.S. nationality** , and against whom the Mexican government has an
**extradition request** before the United States, one that has not been acted
upon because of the impediment this condition represents.

Against that backdrop, Sheinbaum Pardo questioned whether a person with dual
nationality can hold a governorship, and raised the same criterion for the
presidency: “**Why would you have dual nationality if you represent the people
of Mexico?** To be a candidate for governor, why would you hold another
country’s nationality? In other words, **you are Mexican, period**.”

At present, the **Constitution** does not establish a general prohibition on a
person with dual nationality seeking the presidency of the Republic or a
governorship. **Article 30** recognizes who are Mexicans by birth, while
**Article 32** refers to Mexicans who hold another nationality and establishes
that **the law must regulate their rights and prevent conflicts arising from
dual nationality**.

In the case of the presidency, constitutional **Article 82** establishes that
to hold the office one must **be Mexican by birth** , be in full enjoyment of
one’s rights, **be the child of a Mexican father or mother and have resided in
the country for at least 20 years** , although it does not establish a formal
prohibition.

The discussion on the subject has also broadened at the regional level.
Recently the issue sparked debate in Colombia, since the current president,
**Abelardo de la Espriella** , holds **U.S. and Italian** nationalities in
addition to Colombian.

His case generated a legal controversy during the **2026 presidential
campaign** , but the **National Electoral Council** kept his candidacy in
force, and later a **Bogotá court** rejected an action challenging his
election due to his U.S. nationality; this because Colombian legislation
allows Colombians by birth to hold other nationalities and does not establish
that condition as an impediment to serving as President.

A similar case is that of the current **president of Ecuador, Daniel Noboa** ,
who also holds U.S. nationality because he was born in **Miami, Florida**.

In contrast, **Venezuela** does explicitly establish a constitutional
prohibition. **Article 227** of its Constitution states that to be elected
president one **must be Venezuelan by birth and “hold no other nationality”**.

In the Mexican case, an eventual reform would have to define which offices
would be subject to the prohibition; whether the measure would reach people
with **dual nationality acquired by birth** , and how long before an election
renunciation of a second nationality would have to be proven.
